title: New plan to cut daylight saving as two Aussie states endure ‘constant battle’ - Yahoo News Australia
text:
New plan to cut daylight saving as Queensland and NSW endure 'constant battle' - Yahoo News Australia Search query for Search the web Search the web Skip to main 
 News Finance More Mail Search the web Advertisement Advertisement Return to homepage New plan to cut daylight saving as Queensland and NSW endure 'constant battle'
 Millions of Australians could be forced to navigate a new time difference between Sydney and Melbourne under a fresh push to slash daylight saving by two months in NSW.
 Matthew Dunn Fri 20 November 2026 at 6:00 pm UTC 3 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. Millions of Australians could have two fewer months of daylight saving each year under proposed changes to NSW laws. Picture: Getty (Getty) Millions of Australians could see daylight saving cut short by two months under a renewed push that could leave Sydney and Melbourne operating on different time zones for parts of the year.
 NSW Nationals MP Geoff Provest reintroduced legislation to Parliament last Thursday to shorten daylight saving from six months to four , arguing the extended period was disrupting the lives of families, workers and businesses.
 "It is just too damn long," he told NSW Parliament.
 Under the proposed new laws, daylight saving would begin on the first Sunday in November instead of October and finish on the first Sunday in March instead of April.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Provest, whose electorate borders Queensland, said residents were fed up with having to navigate two different time zones for half the year.
 "It is a constant battle to know something as fundamental as what time it is," he said.
 The situation is so problematic that some NSW businesses, including the popular Twin Towns club, operate on Queensland time despite being located just south of the border.
 Do you have a daylight saving story? Contact newsroomau@yahoonews.com 
 Under the proposed changes, NSW residents would wind their clocks back in March instead of April, potentially leaving Sydney and Melbourne an hour apart. Picture: Getty
 (Getty) Why some Aussies want daylight saving cut short
 While many Australians relish the extra daylight after work, the six-month period has long been a source of frustration for those living in regional and border communities.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement For families living along the NSW-Queensland border, even simple tasks such as dropping children at school, attending medical appointments and getting to work can become complicated.
 Cudgen resident Cheryl Hines described the time difference as "a daily logistical hurdle" in a letter read out in NSW Parliament last week.
 Her husband works in Queensland, while she regularly crosses the border to help her elderly mother attend cancer treatment and specialist appointments.
 "Managing these vital medical schedules while trying to return to NSW for my own commitments is a constant source of frustration," she said.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Her daughter, a single mother who lives in NSW and works in Queensland, also faces difficulties collecting her child from after-school care before it closes.
 The prolonged period has also drawn opposition from rural communities, where later sunrises can mean children are travelling to school in darkness.
 Earlier this year, independent MP Helen Dalton raised concerns in parliament about the impact of late sunrises on families in western NSW.
 Hundreds of thousands drawn into daylight saving debate
 Provest said the proposed changes had attracted considerable attention on social media.
 Three Facebook posts promoting the bill collectively attracted more than 260,000 views and 2,300 comments, with the MP claiming most were supportive of the proposed changes.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "Many comments called for daylight saving to be scrapped altogether," he said.

 However, the proposed overhaul could shift the problem currently experienced along the Queensland border to communities straddling the NSW and Victorian border.
 Daylight saving start and finish dates were aligned across NSW, Victoria and the ACT in 2007, with the arrangement taking effect in 2008.
 "There is no reason the alignment cannot continue if the same two-month reduction proposed by this bill is implemented in the ACT and Victoria to continue the time-zone alignment in those southern areas of New South Wales," he said.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement The latest bill is yet to pass parliament.
